name: container-component
intent: Keep presentation state and its access to a data source in an outer wrapper component, so that the components rendering the markup stay stateless functions of the data they are handed.
problem: The same state, or the same data source, is needed by several components below a point in the tree: state ends up duplicated in siblings, intermediate components forward props they never use, and every new field forces edits through components that do not care about it.
context: Declarative component frameworks with props/state and a re-render step - web UI frameworks, mobile declarative toolkits, server-rendered view hierarchies and data-app frameworks with a session cursor. It applies when a subtree needs a shared state owner or a data-fetching wrapper, when children must stay reusable and renderable from plain data, and when the source (store, API, session, fixture) should be swappable without touching the markup.
benefits: Children stay pure functions of their input, so they render from literals in tests, previews and design tools without mocking a store or a network.
One wrapper owns the subscription or data access for a whole subtree, so loading, error and retry handling are written once instead of being duplicated per widget.
The same stateless children can be driven by different sources - live store, server payload, fixture - by writing a different wrapper rather than editing the markup.
The wrapper is the seam where the data source is injected, which keeps framework plumbing (lifecycle, bindings, store subscription) in one file and the subtree testable.
Markup and layout work can proceed without knowing where the data comes from, so design and non-domain contributors can change the view without touching the container.
The split makes it natural to co-locate tests with the code they verify: pure unit tests for stateless children, integration tests with a fixture source for the container.
tradeoffs: One extra layer and one more file per data source; when a single component is the only consumer, the wrapper is overhead with no reuse payoff.
Children still receive data as props or parameters, so deep trees need another channel (context, slot, dependency injection) or the forwarding through intermediate components returns.
The boundary is a convention, not a compiler check: unmanaged codebases drift into container sprawl, or into children that read the data source directly.
State owned higher re-renders a larger subtree, so the pattern costs render work unless children are memoised or state is kept close to its readers.
Subscriptions and listeners created by the wrapper leak unless they are released on the framework's cleanup hook; the lifetime bugs concentrate in the container.
Hooks, state hoisting and retained-binding frameworks reach the same separation with less structure, so applying the split dogmatically adds ceremony rather than clarity.
Where a state holder already exists (ViewModel, Bloc, store, session), the wrapper can quietly duplicate it and become a second, competing model layer.
Containers that over-fetch and pass large snapshots force children to re-render on unrelated field changes, negating the performance intent of the split.

participants.responsibility: Owns the state or subscribes to the data source, performs the data access and side effects, and renders the children with the resulting values and callbacks.
Renders from the values it receives, holds no data source and no subscription, and reports user intent through the callbacks it was given.
The store, API client, session or model the container reads or subscribes to; it can be replaced - live, stub or fixture - without touching the children.
The declared interface between the two roles (values down, events up) that makes a child reusable across containers.
The place that decides which container wraps which children - route, page, screen, dependency-injection wiring or the test fixture.

use_cases: A screen where several widgets need the same live data: one container owns the subscription and renders every widget from the fetched snapshot.
A reusable list, table or form that must render identically from a live store, a server payload and a literal fixture in tests.
A route or page entry that owns navigation parameters and data fetching while its children stay presentation-only.
A form whose draft state and validation live in a wrapper while the fields are stateless inputs driven by value plus change handlers.
A data or terminal application page where session-scoped state drives plain render helper functions.
A legacy or framework-agnostic subtree whose markup is reused by two different data sources (desktop shell and web shell).
A real-time dashboard where a container subscribes to a WebSocket or streaming endpoint and fans the resulting data out to multiple visualization widgets.
A multi-tenant application where the container injects tenant context (ID, permissions, theme) from a session or JWT into a reusable child tree.
A/B or feature-flag experiments where the container resolves the active variant and passes it as a prop to the same stateless content.

A Redux screen where connect() wraps a view component: the wrapper subscribes to the store via mapStateToProps and passes bound action creators as props, so the wrapped component never imports the store.

A Relay page where each subtree declares its data needs with createFragmentContainer and one QueryRenderer at the root fetches the composed query, so children render guaranteed fragment data without fetching anything.

An Angular app using NgRx where smart components inject the Store and pipe selector observables into presentational children, with NgRx ComponentStore owning feature-local state that cleans up on component destroy.
avoid_when: One component is the only consumer of the data and nothing is reused: keep the state in that component.
The framework already separates logic from view without an extra layer (custom hooks, state hoisting, viewmodel bindings): use that idiom directly.
Children already receive everything as explicit input and no data source is involved - a purely presentational tree needs no container.
The state is local and short-lived (hover, animation, an open/closed toggle): keep it in the leaf instead of moving the problem up.
An existing state holder (store, ViewModel, Bloc, session) already owns the same state for the subtree; a second wrapper competes with it.
anti_patterns: Container sprawl: one wrapper per field or per source, until the screen is mostly plumbing and the markup becomes untestable glue.
Half-migrated separation: children take the state as input but also read the store or the network directly when it is convenient.
Copying props into the child's own state, which freezes the value and silently ignores later updates.
Wrappers that only fetch while loading, error and empty states are handled inside the stateless children.
Applying the split dogmatically to a small application where one component with local state is clearer.
Over-fetching containers: passing an entire data snapshot instead of a minimal slice, causing unnecessary re-renders in children that only read one field.
Prop drilling through a container to grandchildren without lifting state higher or introducing a context provider.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: state, data access and side effects on one side, rendering on the other.
Single source of truth: each piece of state has exactly one owner and children never duplicate it.
Dependency inversion: children depend on their input contract, not on a concrete store or API.
Open/closed: new data sources arrive as new wrappers around unchanged children.
Unidirectional data flow: values down, events up - children never mutate what they were given.
Information hiding: children do not know whether the data came from a cache, a network call, a store or a fixture.
Minimal prop surface: the container passes each child only the slice of state that child actually needs, not the whole snapshot.
best_practices: Keep children stateless and pure: values and callbacks only, no data-source imports and no ambient lookups.
Let the wrapper own the subscription lifecycle and release it in the framework's cleanup hook (unmount, dispose, onCleared, effect cleanup).
Name and place the roles consistently (for example containers/ against components/) so the convention is legible, and enforce it with a lint rule if the team depends on it.
Inject the data source into the wrapper so tests and stories can pass a fixture instead of a live store.
Keep one wrapper per data source or state concern rather than per field, and pass each child the smallest slice it needs.
Keep state as close as possible to its readers: a container is for shared or external state, while local UI state stays in the leaf.
Memoise children that receive large or frequently changing data so owning state high does not re-render the whole subtree.
Use a typed contract (interface, protocol, type) for the props so drift between container and child is a compile-time rather than runtime error.
Test containers via integration tests with a fixture source; test presenters via pure unit tests with literal props.
Handle loading, error and empty states explicitly in the container so children receive defined data shapes rather than partial or undefined values.
For real-time sources (WebSockets, streaming), batch or debounce updates to avoid re-rendering on every single data point.
Prefer a single container per subtree that fans out to multiple children over nested containers, to limit the prop-drilling surface.
